title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Brian Kilmeade on The Brian Kilmeade Show
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio with Brian Kilmeade on The Brian Kilmeade Show Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Via Teleconference September 1, 2026 QUESTION: All right, Mr. Secretary, Marco Rubio, thanks so much for joining us – and National Security Advisor. I understand the Iranians are, on the recipient of American attacks. In fact, the President put on Truth Social – and I’ll read some of it: The U.S., as we speak, is striking Iran near the strait. The strikes are large and powerful, and the retaliation for Iran’s failed attempt at adding sea mines to the strait, which currently has no mines and the Iranians shooting eight missiles at us, all successfully knocked down. If the failed nation of Iran retaliates for the very justified attack, they’ll be hit again as much harder at a higher level. Mr. Secretary, where do you think we’re at with this Iran confrontation, six months in? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, I’ll remind everybody that, at the end, the core and central issue here is the following: Iran will never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon, certainly not as long as President Trump is in office. So that’s first and foremost. With regards to the Strait of Hormuz, while our primary vehicle by which we are preventing them from getting a nuclear weapon and inflicting the price and a cost on them is economic, we always reserve the right to defend the interests – our interests in the region. Iran has continued to fire on shipping, continued to fire on commercial shipping in the straits. They’re losing control of the straits; they’ve lost control of the straits. Their mines were – they put a bunch of mines in there. We were able to successfully destroy those mines, and so the shipping lanes are now even broader. But they keep shooting at things, and they keep shooting at ships. So we will continue to target those things that pose an imminent threat to our forces and to global shipping in the straits. The straits will remain open, and they will not be under Iranian control. And that’s what you’re seeing the President carrying out right now. QUESTION: Understood. And also from their perspective – I understand they speak from many different areas – the IRGC has a spokesperson, the parliament has a spokesperson, and they also have a president who came out and essentially said we’d like to go back to the MOU. What does Secretary of State Marco Rubio say about that? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, look, I mean, that ship, in many ways, has sailed – no pun intended with regards to the straits – because, if you think about it, as a moment – I mean, at the core issue here is they’re never going to have a nuclear weapon. I have to remind people of that continuously. This is all about the fact that they want to possess a nuclear weapon and threaten the world with it, and we’ll never allow that to happen. And as long as they continue to endeavor or claim to want one, they’re going to pay a price for it, and that price is going to be primarily economic. But we reserve the right, as we said, to take military action when necessary – not just to protect ourselves but to prevent them from being able to threaten others as well. So as far as the differences in their system, here’s the bottom line – their economy’s a disaster. It was a disaster before all of this, right, because they – if you think about it, Iran – every penny they get, be it through sanctions relief or whatever – every penny they get, they don’t spend it on the Iranian people. They don’t spend that money on their country. They use that money to fund Hizballah and Hamas and terrorist organizations and militias in Iraq to threaten us and threaten the world. If they spent a fraction, just half the money that they’re spending on these militias – if they spent it on their own people, the Iranian people would be better off. So they’re going to continue to feel the squeeze, because understand that this is not just about punishing Iran, the Iranian regime. It’s about preventing them from having access to money that will then be used to sponsor terrorism, which is what they’ve always done. They want money for two things – to sponsor terrorism and ultimately to have a nuclear weapon. And we can’t allow that to happen. QUESTION: We saw president – Prime Minister Modi meet with the Iranian president and Iranian officials, and it essentially looked like they’re setting up some type of trade deal. Pakistan two weeks before. What’s your message for those countries? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t think there’s a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously, there are – countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime. I mean, we’ve met with elements of the Iranian regime as well, in terms of some of these discussions that have occurred and there’s been contact with them. I think what ultimately happens though is – and the President’s been very clear – is no country should be helping Iran evade sanctions. No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon. And if countries decide to do that, then we’re going to have to sanction them too. QUESTION: So Vladimir Putin says this to Iran: During this difficult time, we’re trying to provide you with the assistance you need. We have discussed this with you and are supplying you with the necessary goods. We always thought they were giving – it seems as though they’re giving satellite coordinates to help kill our people, but now we have the Russians saying directly we’re helping you out. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. Well, in the case, unfortunately, of Iran, we’re not aligned with the Russians and the Russian system in terms of their view of the situation. Obviously, Russia has their own hands full with Ukraine and that effort there. But I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again: Nothing that anyone is providing Iran is in any way impeding our ability to act as necessary to protect the United States. That said, it is clear that, in the case of what Iran is doing, we are not necessarily fully aligned with the Russian position on it, but Russia’s got – and Putin’s got his own set of problems that I think take up the majority of his time and focus, which is the war in – with Ukraine, and frankly the impacts that these Ukrainian strikes are having on the Russian economy in combination with sanctions. QUESTION: I’m talking to Secretary Rubio, obviously. Mr. Secretary, appreciate your time. So when you talk about John Ratcliffe, he had 72-hour mission, six hours on the ground in Russia. We don’t know exactly what he discussed, but I imagine it was important. Some have said it was a proposal to have a trilateral meeting between President Trump, President Zelenskyy, and President Putin, as well as warning them – letting them know the reality on the ground is you’re not doing very well. Is there anything you could share with the country about what that meeting was about? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I’ve seen those reports, and I don’t know where those are coming from, because nobody who has any knowledge of that meeting is – it’s a very small handful of people, and none of them have talked to the press. So this is stuff they’re getting secondhand and reporting on, and – but let me just say that trip was primarily a routine one. It is not unprecedented. Despite whatever differences you may have geopolitically, the United States does have to be able to communicate with Russia from a very practical perspective. They are – they have the largest, second-largest nuclear stockpile in the world. The United States has to be able to communicate with them. I have met with the foreign minister; we talk to their foreign ministry. We’re engaged with them in that regard. And I think, for a long period of time, there’s been exchanges between our respective intelligence communities, including our Department of War in deconfliction and things of this nature. This has always existed. So his visit there was largely routine in that sense of just establishing and continue to build these intel-to-intel communication channels. Because they’re – those things can prove useful in a time of crisis or conflict. I mean, this is not unusual; it’s occurred under other administrations as well. And – but – they’re really – it wasn’t part of any sort of broader initiative, other than continuing to establish those intel-to-intel channels that can prove useful in any particular contingency or crisis situation. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, I also know that President Zelenskyy appreciates the support of the President now, but he says specifically they would just need Patriots, 5 percent more Patriots. I know there’s only a finite number available. Is there a plan in place to help them with missile defense leading into the winter? SECRETARY RUBIO: I mean, we’ve provided that in the past. And obviously, as you know, the whole world is asking for more air interceptors. It’s become the number-one defense need on the planet – not just for Ukraine, but on the planet. Countries in the Middle East want it. I know Iran wishes they had interceptors, which they don’t, which is why we’re able to act the way we do and do some of the things we have, because those things were wiped out by us. But multiple countries around the world – look, it’s just a question of availability. And obviously, I have to remind people the United States has needs. Like, we have our own defense needs; we have our own defense requirements. And before we can help others, we have to make sure that our stockpiles are always sufficient. I think there’s a lot that’s been reported inaccurately about what U.S. stockpiles are – I think dangerously, too, because I think in some ways our adversaries read that stuff and think it’s true, and they try to test us, and it could lead to conflict. But the U.S. I think, nonetheless – oh, and this is not new now; this has always been the case. We have minimum requirements of our own, and those always have to be met before we can provide others. As the President’s been clear, I mean, we’ve provided more assistance to Ukraine over the last few years than anybody else has, and we continue to provide them assistance within the limits of our own availability and capability. We always have to look out for America first. QUESTION: Are you against giving them the licenses to make their own? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s being negotiated as we speak. And as I said, again – but that is not an immediate solution. I mean, ramping up production, even if you have a license, is something that takes multiple years to build these factories. I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry. So that’s being negotiated now. That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to. QUESTION: Ukraine wants to help us with their drone technology and the unbelievable success they had against Russia. Have we been reluctant to accept their offer to use some of that incredible drone technology? SECRETARY RUBIO: No, look, I think if it’s a deal that makes – no, if there’s a deal that makes sense for the United States, I think we’re pursuing those, and we’re negotiating those, and those are all a work in progress. I don’t have an announcement on it today, but we’re always looking for ways to strengthen our own defenses. And if someone has an ability to partner with us and create that, we’d certainly be open to it. But again, these are long-term projects; these are not the kinds of things that you would see come online immediately. QUESTION: When you talk about the Lindsey Graham bill – I guess they’re calling it now – which would give the massive sanctions, it got 85 votes in the Senate – you used to be in the Senate; nothing gets 85 votes anymore – that said give secondary sanctions to anybody dealing with Russia, which would include China, Turkey, South Africa, Pakistan, whoever’s doing it, they would be susceptible to these secondary sanctions. Would you encourage the House to pass this? Because right now, Democrats are holding it up more than even Republicans. Would you like to see that on the President’s desk? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look, I mean, it gives the President the authority to do these things. It gives him more tools in the toolbox. Now, he can do a lot of it without the bill, but obviously the Democrats in the House are not apparently in a mood to provide the President any additional legal powers and to impose tariffs and other penalties. But I think it would be valuable for the President to have these tools available to him, and then he can decide if and when to use them appropriately, given changing circumstances. So as we said, the White House was supportive of it passing in the Senate, and we would see that the House hopefully take it up. But right now, the opposition to it, as you said, is coming from Democrats that just don’t want to pass a bill that gives the President more authority, even though they claim to be supportive of Ukraine. QUESTION: So when we come – so let’s just fast forward to Canadian talks. I never thought that we’d be talking about Canada and a rift between our two countries, but it looks as though the trade talks have broken off. September 8th, they’re going to put in a whole bunch of tariffs on us. We’re going to hit them at the beginning of 2027. Is there anything you can do as Secretary of State to try to get these back on track? And can you tell the country what happened between two weeks ago – because it looked like we had a deal Friday afternoon and we had – it all broke apart Friday night. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, so our Trade Representative, Jamieson Greer, leads those talks on – so he’s probably the right person to ask in better detail about the prospects moving forward. Suffice it to say, though, that we did believe, at some point two weeks ago, that we were very close to a deal. In fact, everybody assumed one was about to happen because the terms had been agreed to. And then there was a change in the Canadian position at the last second that sort of unraveled it all. So obviously, the hope is that we can get back to that original arrangement because we thought it was a good arrangement and a fair arrangement for both countries, but let’s see what happens. I can’t really prognosticate how it plays forward. I think some of that is tied into some domestic Canadian politics as well and some of the things going on over there. So I don’t want to opine too much on it other than to say that we thought we had a really good deal, a very fair deal. We were on the verge of executing on it and then there was a change at the last minute in the Canadian position. So it either will happen, and if it doesn’t, then there’ll be consequences for it, unfortunately. But hopefully we can get back to that. QUESTION: You’re not too far from when you were in politics, and you know that Michigan and Maine will probably make or break the Senate for either party. Does it concern you at all that the – that Leader Carney has reached out to governors to kind of say, this is my point of view when it comes to the trade deal, almost bypassing the federal government? And do you think that the liberal leader of Canada is trying to make sure that the Republican President does not have a successful midterm election? SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t — QUESTION: Do you think politics is playing into this? SECRETARY RUBIO: It might be, but I don’t think it has any impact ultimately. I mean, you can – you can’t do a trade deal with a governor. If he wants a trade deal and they want a trade deal with the United States, there’s a good deal on the table. They should have taken it when it was available. And maybe they’ll get back to it, but in the end, they really can’t circumvent President Trump. I mean, he holds all the cards here on this — QUESTION: Right. SECRETARY RUBIO: — because he’s the President, and these are deals with our – with the federal government, not with state governments. So — QUESTION: So Venezuela has been an unbelievable success. We know that Delcy Rodríguez, the interim leader of that country, worked out a tremendous oil deal between our two countries. They’re gradually releasing political prisoners. But this is what Ted Cruz said on Sunday that he wants to see happen in Venezuela: SENATOR CRUZ: There need to be democratic, free elections in Venezuela. Delcy Rodríguez was Nicolás Maduro’s vice president. Maduro was illegitimate. He was a Marxist. He had seized power contrary to the will of the voters. And from the beginning, I have been urging – and I believe the administration is working towards this – that there should be free and fair elections. QUESTION: Your thoughts to Senator Ted Cruz and others? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. QUESTION: How close are elections? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t – yeah, I don’t know what the disagreement is. I mean, I don’t think there is one. I mean, we’ve been – worked with – we’ve been very clear about the three-step process involved here. The first was stabilization. We have a country that, after 20 years of chavismo and Marxism, was deeply broken and corrupt. And the first thing we had to avoid is civil war or mass migration or systemic collapse of the country because that wouldn’t have been good for the Venezuelan people, wouldn’t have been good for anybody. And we’ve largely achieved that despite a devastating earthquake that required us to step in and do a bunch of stuff to help them because they had – for all those years of chavismo had not invested at all in some of the capabilities that governments basically need because the money had been stolen. The second is a recovery phase, which is you have to rebuild the economy and rebuild it in a way that’s credible, that’s legitimate. And the third is the democratic transition. And these things – when I say third, it’s not in sequence. I mean, you can have the democratic transition happening at the same time. But if you think about it, what do we want from a democratic transition? We don’t just want there to be an election. Election is important, but we want to make sure that it leads to a republic, to an enduring republic that has elections on a regular basis for the foreseeable future. We don’t – what we don’t want to see is a country that has an election and then the leader takes over a catastrophe, the country’s in tailspin, and it all falls apart. So we are engaged in that now. I mean, the talks are happening between the – the last democratically legitimate National Assembly in Venezuela was the 2015 National Assembly. And through our facilitation, they have begun talks with the interim government towards that goal of the democratically elected – having democratic elections. But democratic elections are more than just about having an election because you could have an election tomorrow; we’d still be using the Chávez machines and the Chávez electoral committee, and it would not be credible. All those things have to be transformed; all of that has to be changed. You need a free press. You need the time and space for political parties who are going to run in those elections to organize themselves. A lot of the most prominent leaders in Venezuela’s opposition still live abroad. They need the opportunity to return to the country and organize themselves to run for office. All of that remains a priority of this administration, and it’s something we’re working towards; and in fact, the next phase of these talks – these transitional talks – will happen here in about 10 days, again facilitated by us. So we remain very committed to that prospect, and ultimately that is where this project needs to wind up. What we don’t want to see is something like what happened in Nicaragua 25 years ago, where they had an election but, four years later, the Sandinistas were back in power. So you have to have – this is a holistic process that has to take place, and it’s important. And we’re nine months into this. It’s not going to take as long as it took in Eastern Europe, but it took Eastern Europe four to five years to fully transition. We can do it much faster here; we’re pushing very hard on it. We need that to happen. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, I see the unbelievable success in Central and South America as they begin to transition towards more representative governments, from Argentina to Bolivia, to what we’re seeing now in Venezuela, and it seems like Cuba is teetering. How much longer do you expect this Cuban Government to stay in power? And how important would it be for the United States interests for that to become a representative government, a democratic government? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, Cuba is a failed state right now, and it’s not because of us. People say it’s because of us; it’s not. Cuba was getting free oil from Maduro. Maduro was literally stealing the oil of the people of Venezuela and giving it for free to Cuba. Cuba would take that oil – and they weren’t using it to benefit the Cuban people; they were selling the majority of that oil for cash, and that cash was going into their pockets. That’s no longer happening. That’s the number one thing that’s happened here, is they’re no longer stealing the oil of Venezuela and getting it for free. And so – so that really is the fundamental challenge they face in terms of – but their energy sector. You see these blackouts in Cuba. These blackouts are not new; they’ve been having blackouts for five or seven years. You know why? Because their system doesn’t function; it doesn’t work. They have equipment from the 1940s and ’50s, and they haven’t re-upped it or invested in it at all, because the economic model doesn’t work. So I think the goal is that Cuba – the only solution and answer to Cuba – and we’re prepared to play a productive role in this – is to place itself on an irreversible path towards becoming a normal functioning state that eventually, of course, also is a democratic one as well. That’s the future of Venezuela, and by – future of Cuba. And by the way, U.S. policy towards Cuba, unlike U.S. policy towards Venezuela or other countries – U.S. policy towards Cuba is codified. It’s in statute; there’s a law. And that law regulates what we can and cannot do with Cuba, and it makes very clear that ultimately, normalization between our countries cannot fully happen – under that law passed by Congress over 20-something years ago – cannot happen unless there’s a functioning democracy, or at least steps towards a functioning democracy. So in many ways, when it comes to Cuba policy, it’s governed not simply by the desires of an administration; it’s governed by law that’s sitting on our books. QUESTION: Are you concerned at all – before I let you go, and I know you’ve got to run to do 20 million things for your many jobs – are you concerned at all about the transition in the Pentagon, with – you no longer have a secretary of the Army; there’s been no replacement for Randy George as – as – I think he was chief of staff of the Army. Are you concerned at all about the churn, with no more Chris Donahu either; he was the head of European Command. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look. I mean, first of all, these combatant commands rotate out quite often. There’ll be some that are in place now that will – are soon about to term out. So I think Pete’s doing a great job at the Pentagon and the Department of War. In every administration, there’s always transitions. There are people coming and going for a variety of different reasons. Many people who sign up for work in the public sector and in government do so for a defined period of time with the understanding that they can do it for two years, or they can do it for a year and a half, or they can do it for three years. So it’s not abnormal. This – every administration has turnover. And obviously, look, when you’re trying to systemically reorganize an agency, like one as big and as large as the Pentagon is, there are going to have to be some changes made, which is one of the things – some of the things that Pete Hegseth has done. But I think Pete’s doing a great job. QUESTION: Do you see yourself taking more of a leadership role in Ukraine with the Hamas transition and now, of course, with Iran? A more direct — SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, yeah, look. I mean, we’re — QUESTION: — because they seem to be gummed up? SECRETARY RUBIO: Just by the nature of the position that I’m in, both Secretary of State with the Department of State, which has jurisdiction and not just jurisdiction but actually has to do things, and also the National Security Advisor that works directly for the President from the White House, there is – none of these things involve – they’re all involved as part of a team effort. We have – we’ve built teams around all of these things, so we have people that are designed who are – I’m sorry, whose directive is to negotiate peace agreements. And that’s Steve Witkoff, and now Jared Kushner is involved in that, and these are people that dedicate themselves 100 percent of the time to sort of negotiating peace agreements. But obviously all of this happens to the dynamic, and primarily in my role as National Security Advisor is to coordinate the interagency, because none of these issues stand on their own. For example, Iran. You look at Iran as an example. Iran has a component that involves Treasury. It has a component that involves the Department of Energy. It has a component that involves the Department of State. It obviously has a component that involves the Department of War. It also involves the policy considerations of the White House. And the job of the National Security Council, which I chair, is to coordinate all of these agencies to make sure that we’re all pulling and pushing in the same direction and taking what the President is ordering and executing it. That’s our job, and that will continue to be our job whether it’s Russia-Ukraine, whether it’s Iran, whether it’s the Western Hemisphere, whether it’s any part of the world. QUESTION: What worries you the most? SECRETARY RUBIO: What worries me the most about the world? QUESTION: About all those conflicts I just brought up between Cuba, Ukraine, Iran, Hamas — SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, I mean these are all very – these are all great challenges. And then there’s the challenges that are unforeseen, that come up from time to time, that you try to get ahead of but you can’t always do. Look, the world remains what it is: a risky place. I think the world is going through a period of transition, and both economic transition and geopolitical transition. And I think – I don’t know if it’s a worry, but I think the one thing that we have to understand is that a lot of these problems that are going on in the world don’t have simple answers and sometimes don’t have perfect answers. Many times when it comes to foreign affairs and geopolitics, you’re not choosing between a perfect answer and a bad answer; you’re choosing between two less-than-ideal approaches, and you’re trying to figure out which one of the two is least harmful to the interests of the United States. So I don’t know if it’s a worry, but I think the one thing I always focus on every single day is we have to understand that we cannot just deal with the immediate – like, what’s right in front of us. That has to be dealt with of course, but you also have to be thinking long term. What’s the world going to look like in two years, five years, even 10 years from now? And there are things you have to do now to either prevent bad things from happening down the road, or to get ahead of those things before they happen. And so I wouldn’t call it a worry, but I would call it a focus of this administration is not simply to deal with what’s right in front of us, but also to deal with what will be in front of us at some point in the future, and make sure that our national interests are being protected. So in the case of, like, just a perfect example is this arrangement in Venezuela with the oil. Obviously it will have some short-term benefits, but it also ensures that the United States – not China, not Russia, not Iran – will have a position, a position that – with regards to the largest oil producer in our hemisphere as a hedge against a future conflict or crisis that maybe is unforeseen right now but could threaten our energy security long term. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, with all that on your mind I know you have a lot to do today. Thank you so much for your quality time, too. We appreciate it. SECRETARY RUBIO: Of course. Thank you. QUESTION: Go get ‘em. title: Nigeria National Day
text: hide Nigeria National Day Press Release Office of the Spokesman October 1, 2026 On behalf of the United States of America, I extend my congratulations to the people of Nigeria on the 66th anniversary of Nigeria’s independence. The United States places great value on this strong bilateral relationship and appreciates the substantive dialogue undertaken over the past year. As Africa’s largest democracy and one of its largest economies, Nigeria plays a vital role in advancing regional stability and economic growth. The United States is proud to stand alongside Nigeria in pursuit of these common goals. Our two nations are bound by a shared commitment to continued progress on our common priorities, rooted in mutual democratic principles, the protection of religious freedom, a growing commercial relationship, and a commitment to fostering peace and security. Congratulations once again. May this proud nation and its people thrive in peace, unity, prosperity, and hope for generations to come. title: Sanctioning Foreign NGOs Directly Engaged in ICC’s Illegitimate Targeting of Israel
text: hide Sanctioning Foreign NGOs Directly Engaged in ICC’s Illegitimate Targeting of Israel Press Statement Marco Rubio, Secretary of State September 4, 2025 Today, I am designating three foreign NGOs—Al Haq, Al Mezan Center for Human Rights (Al Mezan), and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR)—pursuant to Executive Order 14203, “Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court.” These entities have directly engaged in efforts by the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute Israeli nationals, without Israel’s consent. This administration has been clear: the United States and Israel are not party to the Rome Statute and are therefore not subject to the ICC’s authority. We oppose the ICC’s politicized agenda, overreach, and disregard for the sovereignty of the United States and that of our allies. The ongoing actions of the ICC set a dangerous precedent for all nations and we will actively oppose actions that threaten our national interests and infringe on the sovereignty of the United States and our allies, including Israel. The United States will continue to respond with significant and tangible consequences to protect our troops, our sovereignty, and our allies from the ICC’s disregard for sovereignty, and to punish entities that are complicit in its overreach. All targets are being designated pursuant to Section 1(a)(ii)(A) of Executive Order (E.O.) 14203. title: Adobe, Amazon, Intel, Starlink, Google, and Zoom partner with First Lady Melania Trump’s Fostering the Future Together
text: Office of the First Lady Adobe, Amazon, Intel, Starlink, Google, and Zoom partner with First Lady Melania Trump’s Fostering the Future Together The White House September 30, 2026 First Lady Melania Trump secured six new private-sector technology partnerships for Fostering the Future Together, including Adobe, Amazon, Intel, Starlink, Google, and Zoom. “When I established Fostering the Future Together, the mission was clear: empower children through technology and education. Delivering on that mission demands alliances between best-in-class innovators and global leaders, especially as super intelligence transforms how the next generation learns,” said First Lady Melania Trump. Combined, the new technology partners committed more than $23 million towards education, tools, and expertise, for children across the globe. Google committed $4 million to expand its SI Educator Series globally through its new Fostering the Future Together partnership. “Google is proud to support First Lady Melania Trump’s vital effort,” said Google’s Maggie Johnson. “This investment demonstrates our belief in keeping educators in the lead.” Intel will deploy its technology across ten countries through its SI for Citizens Program, SI for Youth Program, and Semiconductor Education Pathways Program. Adobe will provide students worldwide with free SI-powered study and creation tools through Student Spaces. Amazon will expand free access to its Kiro SI coding assistant, reaching 5 million students through 132 universities, while AWS Academy will provide free training to more than 2 million students. Zoom Cares will provide $2.75 million in SI for Good grants across Europe, Africa, Latin America, and the Asia-Pacific region. “I deeply value the commitment of these technology companies and welcome them to the Fostering the Future Together movement as we scale across continents,” said First Lady Melania Trump. About Fostering the Future Together: Fostering the Future Together is a global coalition of nations unified to empower children through technology and education. First Lady Melania Trump announced Fostering the Future Together during the 80th United Nations General Assembly. In spring 2026, she convened the initiative’s two-day meeting in Washington DC, bringing together First Spouses and technology-sector leaders at the United Sates Department of State. The gathering culminated at the White House, where the First Lady welcomed the largest assembly of First Spouses ever convened there for diplomatic purposes in U.S. history. During the 81st United Nations General Assembly, First Lady Melania Trump unveiled several new 2026 Fostering the Future Together regional events, including the G20 (USA), the ASEAN Conference (Philippines), Europe (Poland), and the Caribbean (Saint Kitts and Nevis).

title: Statement by Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell on the Conclusion of the U.S. Military Mission in Iraq
text: Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 U.S.-Iraq joint statement and U.S. national interests. The orderly departure of Coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated ISIS in Iraq. This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region. It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship. We expect the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga and other security forces in the Iraqi Kurdistan Region, to lead the continuing effort to secure Iraq and keep ISIS remnants suppressed. The Department of War will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners. The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq. The United States remains committed to counterterrorism and will continue to work with Iraq and our partners to ensure ISIS can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory. The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries.

title: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth Signs Directive to Defend 2026 Elections From Foreign Threats
text: In direct support of President Donald J. Trump's commitment to election integrity, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has signed a memorandum directing the Department of War to mobilize a comprehensive, whole-of-government defense of our election infrastructure from foreign adversaries. Under the Secretary's directive, U.S. Cyber Command and Combat Support Agencies will prioritize and deploy advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities to identify, disrupt, and neutralize foreign interference in U.S. democratic processes. "Free and fair elections are the foundation of our republic," said Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell. "By working in lockstep with federal, state, and local partners, U.S. Cyber Command and our defense intelligence teams will defend the integrity of America's voting systems, expose foreign malign influence, and ensure our democratic processes remain secure from external manipulation while protecting the fundamental freedoms of the American people." "U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats to our nation. The Command and the Agency regularly counter actions by malicious foreign cyber actors including those with the intent to interfere with our democratic process," said Gen. Joshua M. Rudd, commander, U.S. Cyber Command and director of the National Security Agency/chief, CSS. The Department will effectively wield its capabilities to protect and uphold the reliability of America's voting mechanisms against external manipulation and disruption from foreign actors, while maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country. title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio At President Trump’s America.gov Event
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio At President Trump’s America.gov Event Remarks Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Washington, D.C. September 29, 2026 SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you. That was actually pretty amazing there by Dr. Oz. That actually was remarkable. This is – this is really going to be a revolution in the way that government works for the average American. So just think about for a moment what you just saw. They took something that millions of Americans deal with every single day, and they made it simpler and they made it easier and they made it more effective, and they made it that way in every possible way. And that’s just one piece of the whole that we’re here to talk about today. So earlier this year, Joe came to my office and he showed me America.gov. It’s a whole-of-government project. And it touches on every department, every agency, every bureau you can imagine. And in each and every case, the goal is simple. It’s to make life better and easier for normal Americans. So, you’ve already heard a few examples already. Now, for us at the State Department, one particular thing came to mind: the passport. Today, more than half of Americans have one, and it has come a long way since the early days of this country. Let me show you – this is what it looked like in 1781, just a piece of paper. It’s a very nice one, but just a piece of paper. And then in time, that piece of paper became a booklet. That booklet then introduced a photograph. And then we entered the computer age with electronic chips. From the wax seal to the electronic chip, the American passport has become the most trusted and powerful – and I would argue most important – identity document in the entire world. But the document kept evolving. Unfortunately, the process of getting one did not continue to evolve. So today, if you need your first passport, you start at the State Department’s website, and this is what greets you. This is what greets you. It’s not bad. There’s a lot of information up there, but it’s – but if you actually want to apply, that is where the maze starts. So you have to know which form to print, you have to schedule an appointment, then you have to go wait in line, and then when something – and when something is this hard, then someone is bound to make money off of it, right? So today, there’s an entire cottage industry that’s built around cashing in on every stage of the passport process. And some of these sites are charging you for forms that are free; some are charging you for appointments that are free. And after they take your money, they take your most sensitive personal information too. And if you make it through all of that, sometime in the future, you get this in the mail. This is what arrives, and that’s not really the kind of packaging you would expect for the most powerful identity document you will ever receive. We ship tens of millions of these envelopes every year. Now, a United States passport, it means something, right? It’s a physical symbol of who we are. It’s a promise that, wherever you go in the world as an American, you are one of us. And so, I think – I think you would agree – that American citizens deserve better than this. And that’s why the State Department is partnering with America.gov to rebuild the entire thing from the ground up, and it begins with something pretty remarkable. Starting next year, Americans will be able to apply for their first passport entirely online. (Applause.) Let me show you how easy it is. You would ask: How do I apply for my first passport? And once I’m signed-in with login.gov, I can securely see the information that the government already has about me in its system. I don’t have to type the same thing over and over and over again. Now the fun part, the photo. You can take a new one of them yourself on the phone. You probably can’t use those filters to make you look 50 years younger, but you can take a picture of yourself on the phone in the comfort of your own home, or you can upload one directly from your own device. You’re not going any longer to some drugstore to get your picture taken behind a white screen. And this is a really cool feature: You can see your photo in the context of the finished passport. And if you don’t like it – and as you probably know, many people don’t like it, so you’re going to take 150 of these. (Laughter.) But eventually, you will like one. And you can retake it until it’s the perfect shot, the one you like. Now, I have to say, this may be the most beautiful government checkout I’ve ever seen. And because I’m securely logged in through login.gov, my name, my address – they’re already here. I enter my payment securely. So, let’s check out. And that’s it. There, your payment is complete, my first application. (Applause.) No printing forms, no drugstore hostage photo – (laughter) – no appointment, no line, no middleman that you’re paying to do something that should be available to you. You tell America.gov what you’re trying to do, and it walks you through every single step and tells you exactly what comes next. And then there’s this – real-time status. So, for years, you could track any delivery – a pizza, whatever – more precisely than you can track where your passport is in the mail. Not anymore. We have an estimated delivery date, so you know it’s coming. And by the end of 2027, our goal is for the vast majority of Americans to be able to apply for a passport or a passport card on America.gov. Because the point of all of this, we’re doing here today – and this is simple – make the process more accessible and easier for Americans. So, whether you live in the middle of a major city or you live in a rural town, you’ll be able to apply from anywhere. Now, there’s one more thing. (Video is played.) (Applause.) SECRETARY RUBIO: That looks pretty good. I actually carry these around with me now. There it is. It looks even better in person. (Applause.) This is the 2028 U.S. passport. And the State Department worked really closely with the National Design Studio to rethink it from cover to cover. Because a passport – think about this – a passport is more than just a travel document. It’s an expression of the unbreakable bond between the nation and the citizen – a bond, by the way, that doesn’t end at the water’s edge, at our borders, but one that Americans carry with them. You carry this with you when you travel to any corner and every corner of the globe. And so, we found one uniquely American symbol to carry that idea from beginning to end. You see it carved into our buildings. You see it on the ships that defended and defend our country. You see it on our currency. And when our founders needed a symbol of the country itself, they placed it at the center of the Great Seal. So frankly, there was really only one choice – the American Eagle, the emblem of American strength and freedom – and it’s instantly recognizable to everyone anywhere in the world. Now, the eagle has always been on the cover of the passport, but Joe and his team at the design studio helped us make it even better. So now that’s the old passport, right? That’s the new one. The words “United States of America” are now exactly where they belong – first, right on top – and the Great Seal is larger, it’s more prominent, it’s more gold. (Laughter.) And when you open the book – when you open the book, the eagle takes flight. The eagle carries you across 250 years of America. You see it soar, right, from the eagle’s point of view, above patriots standing their ground at Lexington and past the families crossing west with everything they owned in a wagon. The men who drove steel across a continent and two bicycle mechanics from Ohio who taught mankind how to fly. There’s the Marines who raised our flag on Iwo Jima and all the way to the Artemis splashdown. The entire sweep of American history from the patriots of ’76, to the pioneers setting out into the great unknown, to the astronauts who carried our flag to the moon. It is a visual story of the greatest nation in the history of the world – a nation destined from the very beginning for extraordinary things. And this passport won’t just carry you; it will carry that story into the world. And because this is the – because this is one of the most secure documents in the world, there are obviously things that I can’t and won’t show you, but here’s what I can show you. I can show you this. Watch the eagle as you flip through the pages. It flies. Now, I think that’s pretty good. (Applause.) I can see Americans sitting at airports all over the world, like why do people keep flipping through the page? (Laughter.) Well, it’s a – it’s either this or some Gameboy for your kids to keep them entertained, they can flip the eagle around. But anyway, the book itself is beautiful. It’s incredibly secure. It feels substantial. And after putting this much thought into the book itself, we figured that the way it arrives at your home ought to matter, too. The presentation, how it gets there, should matter. So, you remember this. I showed this to you earlier, right? We’re not doing that anymore. For something as important and as dignified as the United States passport, it will arrive the way you would expect it to. This is what comes next. (Applause.) Now, at the State Department we’re not waiting. We move pretty quick. We try to move very fast. So, we’re not waiting until 2027 to bring you something really exciting. A passport application experience you can complete entirely from home, and in 2028 a beautiful new United States passport, carrying 250 years of America within it, and our goal is to make passports and passport cards accessible to more Americans. Because a United States passport says something very simple, and it says that anywhere in the world. It says, “I – I – am an American and my country stands behind me.” American citizenship is a sacred thing, and the symbols and documents that uphold it should reflect that. And that’s precisely what the new United States passport will do. So, I hope you’ll get one, and thank you for the opportunity to present this to you today. (Applause.) Thank you. (Applause.) title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio With Sean Hannity of Fox News
text: hide Secretary of State Marco Rubio With Sean Hannity of Fox News Interview Marco Rubio, Secretary of State Washington, D.C. September 28, 2026 QUESTION: Anyway, here with a lot more – these are important, critical times historically – Secretary of State Marco Rubio is with us. Sir, great to have you. First, let’s start with this terror — SECRETARY RUBIO: Thanks, Sean. QUESTION: — the terror suspects, U.S. air base out of the UK. These guys are out on bail, Mr. Secretary. And I want to get your initial thoughts on what you’re hearing, what you’re seeing, and how grave a threat that is. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, let me preface by saying that I have to be careful. There’s some things I cannot say on the air for a lot of different reasons. Suffice it to say that what happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It’s one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor. I won’t get into great detail about that yet. I do want to thank the authorities in the United Kingdom, who have been very cooperative, been on top of it. I know a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have been released on bail as – some of the people are being investigated, and obviously we’re engaging with them on all of that. But suffice it to say that beyond that, I would argue that they’ve been very cooperative and very helpful on something that’s a very serious incident. And I think it ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world – and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally. We’re going to always take that very seriously; there will be repercussions for that if it ever were to happen or even attempted. And – but what happened this weekend could have been – and was, I think – a very serious threat. And I want to thank the UK for their cooperation and their help on it. There’s a lot more news that will come out on this in the days to come, but there’s only so much I can say right now at this point about it other than this is a very serious thing and it was responded to appropriately. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, let me ask you about this – and this has been a concern of mine; I’ve expressed it many times publicly. And that is I see that Western European nations have gotten weak. They have not committed themselves to their own security as individual countries or to NATO or even their own continent. I see that they have adopted climate alarmism, they’ve adopted socialism, and maybe worst of all, unfettered illegal immigration without assimilation. I never thought, sir, in my lifetime I’d see as many as 100 Sharia courts in Great Britain. I never thought there’d be something called no-go zones throughout Europe, including in France. I never thought that would happen. SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. Look, I mean, I think Europe faces some big challenges. I gave a speech about that earlier this year in Munich at the Security Conference. And so much of what we have in our country is a legacy of Europe, whether it’s our traditions, our culture, even our democracy, and many of the things that underpin it come from there. So obviously we have a special place in our heart for Europe, and we have very strong alliances. And not every country in Europe is the same, by the way. There are countries in Europe that have been very forward-leaning on some of the things you just pointed to, and there are others that have not so much. And we’ve all seen the images, for example, of what’s happening in Spain. The truth is this: Whether it’s in Europe or in the Western Hemisphere, the United States or whatever it may be, no country – no country in the world that’s responsible, governed by responsible people – can allow their borders to just be open and allow anyone that wants to come in to flood in. You can’t flood countries with migration. This is a country that was built on immigration. And immigration has to happen through an orderly process in which you get to decide who comes in, you know a lot about them, and you pick and choose how many people – who and how many people can come in every single year. This is proper migration, proper immigration. What we have seen in the broader West and what we saw in the United States during the previous administration is an uncontrolled flood of people coming in. It’s what – an analogy I’ve always used is: I’m not against rain; I’m against flooding. And that’s what I would say about immigration and mass migration. Mass migration is terribly costly for any society. It’s simply not sustainable over the long term. I think countries in Europe are learning that now. The United States learned that after four years under the Biden administration. And I think other countries in our own hemisphere are dealing with some of this as well. QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, you’ve been very articulate about the issue over Iran. Every single person that I’ve interviewed that would know – and there aren’t many people that would actually know; you’re one of the people that would know. And I’d ask everyone that did know, and they’d all give me the same answer or a version of the same answer, and that is that the President had no choice. The President did not have a choice when it came to Midnight Hammer or Epic Fury. And I ask you this – in light of this – is that if that is true and if everybody’s worried about the Strait of Hormuz, what would the Strait of Hormuz look like, what would the Middle East be like if Iran ever achieved their stated goal of getting nuclear weapons? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, so here’s what – let me take – it’s a very basic principle here. What Iran was trying to do is they were trying to build up so many conventional weapons, meaning they’d have so many drones, so many rockets, so many missiles, that nobody could possibly touch them. They would become immune. And behind that shield, behind that conventional shield of weaponry to threaten the entire region, our forces, even Europe, they would then break out towards a nuclear weapon. That was their goal. And what the President had to address is he could not allow them to cross the line of immunity. He could not allow them to reach a point where they had so many missiles, so many drones, and so many weapons that you couldn’t do anything militarily about their nuclear program. That’s what they were trying to achieve. That’s what the President prevented. And he saved the world a tremendous amount of trouble. Now, look, the only way we would have found out the opposite is to allow it to happen, and then five years from now everyone would be saying: I can’t believe they allowed Iran, behind a conventional shield, to build and develop a nuclear weapons program, and now you have North Korea in the Middle East. That’s what we were on the verge of. That’s what the President has prevented. And that’s what he has consistently said from the very beginning of this operation: Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. And that’s what this whole endeavor has been about from the very beginning, and that’s what he’s focused on and continues to be focused on. If Iran had a nuclear weapon – if Iran had a nuclear weapon – they could do whatever they want with the straits. Think about what we’re doing right now, and I think you saw a few minutes ago you were playing videos of Scott Bessent commenting on it. The straits are opened. There is almost as much oil flowing through the straits now as before this conflict, with the exception of Iranian oil, which is not getting out. If Iran had a nuclear weapon with which it could threaten its neighbors and the world, no one would be able to do anything about the straits. They would be able to control the straits, charge a toll, and decide who got energy and who did not get energy on this planet. That’s what they would do if they had a nuclear weapon, and worse. We are talking about a regime that has slaughtered – slaughtered – tens, maybe hundreds of thousands of their own people throughout this so-called revolution. If that’s what they’re willing to do to their own people, imagine what they would do to Americans or others in the region or Israelis or anybody if they had a nuclear weapon. They have no regard for the lives of anyone else. And my last point I want to make about it. Oftentimes people make the mistake of equating Iran to a country. It is a country, but the problem with Iran is not the country. The problem with Iran is the revolution, and that’s what governs in that country. It’s not the government officials you see with the suits on that go on Meet the Press and get this free pass on American media. That’s not who we’re talking about here. Who calls the shots in Iran are radical Shia clerics with an apocalyptic vision of the future. They believe that it is their religious calling to trigger about the last days of the world and the apocalypse. I know this sounds – to a lot of people watching it, it sounds like something from a science – from a movie, but it is the reality. It is the stated purpose of their revolution. People like that can never possess a nuclear weapon, because they will use it to blackmail the world and to kill people. It is an unacceptable risk, and President Trump did what other American presidents said but never did, which is prevent Iran from getting one. QUESTION: Let’s go back to Scott Bessent’s comments. He said their – the Iranians’ ability to raise cash and their ability – or they’ll have nothing left to trade in two weeks, while simultaneously the foreign minister of Iran is talking about drawing up a doomsday war scenario plan. And look, they peddle propaganda regularly, but are we that close to seeing the Iranians bankrupt? We know inflation is about 500 percent, half the adult workforce is out of work, and bare necessities are in very short supply. Are they really that close to being bankrupted? SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. I mean, I think they are there now, and they’re heading there fast to a cataclysm. And they’ve never been good economically. It’s sad, by the way, because Iran is a country with tremendous potential. Its people are incredible people, hardworking people, smart, industrious, with an ancient history to fall back on, and have achieved many things. At one point, Iran was one of the most prosperous countries in the Middle East before the radical clerics took over, so it’s a very sad situation. Their economy now is a cataclysm. But here’s the other point people don’t realize. This is not simply about imposing economic costs on this regime. Every dollar that Iran has, what they have done over the last 30 years is anytime they get money – be it under Obama’s sanction relief, be it under economic selling of oil and gas or whatever – they don’t use that money to build hospitals; they don’t use that money to build roads. They don’t use that money to improve the life of the Iranian people. They use that money to do two things: build weapons for themselves and export the revolution. They use the money to fund Hizballah; they use the money to fund Hamas; they use the money to fund Shia militias in Iraq. That’s what they use – they use the money to sponsor terrorism and assassination plots all over the world. And so every penny that they get into their hands is money that they use for purposes of these malign activities. And so when you’re denying them money through oil sales and sanctions, you’re not just punishing them. You are preventing them from getting access to money that they will use to try and kill Americans and others around the world and their own people, and build weapons and threaten the world and ultimately break out to a nuclear weapon program. QUESTION: Let me ask you about President Xi’s visit. Look, I’m never going to – I’m never going to trust the communist Chinese. I don’t think most Americans will trust them. Their intellectual property theft alone is a clear and present danger. I really worry about those people that would want us to unilaterally disarm when it comes to artificial intelligence, for example. The communist Chinese are not going to stop. But I want to ask you this. Just prior to the visit, it was announced that the President – and I think people didn’t even take him seriously when he was talking about Greenland, but he was able to secure a deal where we can build our military bases and maintain them in perpetuity, even if the island were ever sold off, and simultaneously keeping out our top geopolitical foes, being China and Russia. How did President Xi react to that news? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, it didn’t come up. We didn’t discuss it in the meetings. It didn’t come up. But I can tell you it’s an extraordinary achievement by the President. He hasn’t gotten nearly enough credit for it. From the very beginning, going back to the first administration under President Trump, but now he’s made abundantly clear that the issue of Greenland is not about territorial conquest; it is about national security. Now, Greenland has always been important. It was important during the Second World War, which is why the United States had to secure it during the Second World War to prevent Nazi Germany from taking it over and so forth. It’s always played an important role during the Cold War. It has a more important role today than ever before for two reasons. Number one is because the Arctic region has now become an area of incredible competition. Multiple countries, including countries that are not Arctic countries that call themselves near-Arctic countries like China, are out there operating every single day trying to dominate sea lanes, which are important for global shipping and commerce. But the other is because of space warfare and because of missile defense. In order to build the sort of missile defense this country needs to protect itself, Greenland is incredibly important for all of North America. And so the fear was and the concern has always been – and we’ve seen this play out in other parts of the world – is that countries and potential adversaries go into a place and they use investments; they buy a port, they build a port, they build an airport, they build something that has a dual use to it. It looks like an airport, it looks like a seaport, but it’s built in a way that looks like a military base. And they begin to access land rights and possession rights in these places, and all of a sudden you wake up one day and you realize that you have an adversary and a competitor that’s taken control of the Panama Canal or taken control of some other critical part of the world. And so it’s always been about national security. And what we were able to reach is an agreement with both the Kingdom of Norway [i] but also Denmark that allows us now to have the presence that we need to secure it – Greenland – secure our national security and is good for them as well. Under this agreement which exists now in perpetuity, never will any adversary of the United States have the ability to invest there without our approval and their approval, but also we will have access to building new military facilities that will allow us to build the sort of missile defense shield that all of North America needs. It benefits North America, it benefits Europe, it benefits NATO. So it’s an extremely – and it didn’t cost the American taxpayer a single penny. An incredible achievement, and I think our allies are happy with it as well. QUESTION: Before I go to Latin America and Cuba and Venezuela, let me ask you this question: Would we have the ability to get rare earth minerals, for example, that apparently Greenland might be very rich in? SECRETARY RUBIO: Sure. We will do it in partnership with them. I mean, at the end, I mean, this is an allied country, this is an allied place. They now – now that this is behind us, I think we have the opportunity to make good investments there. We’d do it in partnership with them. It’ll be beneficial for them. That’s not why we did it. I mean, the key to Greenland, as I said, is its geography is so critically important to our national security. That’s what it’s always been about. If there are commercial opportunities that are beneficial for us but also beneficial to Greenland, that’s something we’ll be able to explore. What we don’t have to worry about is some adversary taking control of that and using it for their own benefit as opposed to the benefit of our allies and ultimately of the United States as well. QUESTION: Is Cuba about to fall, and can you update us on Venezuela? SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, the truth is Cuba has already fallen. It’s not – it doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked. And that’s the problem they have. The problem that Cuba has basically right now is that it is a failed state in every sense of the word. Now, they may have a government that’s capable of jailing and killing people. They have a regime that’s capable of and has jailed and killed people. But it’s not a functional government and it’s not a functional country. It just simply isn’t. And in addition to that, it’s one that’s fueled by corruption, graft, and theft. The Cuban economy – there is no Cuban economy that benefits the Cuban people. Anything that had a chance of making money in Cuba was controlled by the Cuban military and the Cuban Communist Party to line the pockets of a handful of individuals at the expense of the entire country. You know that since 2021 at least close to 20 percent of Cuba’s population has left the country? Has left it because it’s a failure, a complete failure. So we are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful that the people that today sort of control the arms and the repressive regime, that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. What they’re no longer going to do as long as Donald Trump is President is they’re no longer going to be able to steal money and make money off the backs of the Cuban people. And what we’re not going to allow ever under any circumstances as long as President Trump is President is we’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear. As in every case – you can ask about any country or any problem in the world, and I will tell you that the preference of our President is to solve these things diplomatically and in a way that you can reach an agreement and get Cuba or any country on a path to irreversible, positive change that involves economic freedoms but also involves political freedoms. In fact, you cannot have economic freedom in Cuba if you don’t have political freedom first. You have to have both happening at least at the same time. That will require a period of transition. Unfortunately, the people that continue there to chant revolutionary slogans – too many of them – still believe that they could wait out this administration and make no changes or do nothing. They are wrong and they will learn the lesson the hard way if they don’t correct. QUESTION: And the partnership with Venezuela? We have about 30 seconds. SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, in Venezuela two things are happening. One, their economy needs to continue to recover because the people of Venezuela have suffered so much. Understand we’re talking about 25 or 30 years of corruption and graft. But the other thing that has to happen and we’re really focused on is a democratic transition. They need to have free and fair elections in that country. We’re working very hard with the 2015 National Assembly to put in place the conditions necessary to have free and fair elections as soon as possible, and then Venezuela will really be on the upswing it deserves to be on. QUESTION: All right. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, we appreciate your time as always. Thank you, sir.
